prompt: Why are oral traditions like Homeric verse built from stock phrases such as 'swift-footed Achilles' and 'wine-dark sea'?
options: The poets had small vocabularies
Formulae aid extempore composition and memory
Greek lacks a written alphabet
Audiences disliked novel language
correctAnswer: Formulae aid extempore composition and memory
explanation: Milman Parry showed in the 1930s that the Homeric epics were built from a vast inventory of pre-fitted formulae sized to fill the metrical line. This allowed bards to compose anew in performance, working from memory without a written text. Oral cultures encode knowledge for the medium — rhythm, meter, formula — because there is no stable text to fall back on.

prompt: The earliest writing in Mesopotamia (cuneiform, c. 3200 BCE) was used primarily for:
options: Religious epics
Love poetry
Accounting and administration
Medical recipes
correctAnswer: Accounting and administration
explanation: The earliest cuneiform tablets are receipts: counts of grain, beer, sheep, and labor owed to temples and palaces. Writing began as a tool of state and temple administration, not literature. Literary, legal, and religious uses came later, riding on a technology first invented for bookkeeping.

prompt: The bound-page book form that gradually replaced the scroll in late antiquity is called the _________.
correctAnswer: codex
explanation: The codex — a stack of folded leaves stitched at one edge — emerged in the early Roman Empire and was adopted enthusiastically by early Christians, in part because it allowed quick cross-reference between different parts of scripture. By late antiquity it had largely displaced the scroll for everyday use, though Torah scrolls preserve the older form to this day.

prompt: Which innovation made literacy practical for non-specialists?
options: The codex
Papyrus
The alphabet
Wood-block printing
correctAnswer: The alphabet
explanation: Logographic systems like Egyptian hieroglyphs or Chinese characters require thousands of distinct signs, restricting full literacy to specialists. The alphabet — Phoenician (c. 1050 BCE), then Greek (with vowels added) — uses ~22–26 reusable symbols. This compactness made it feasible for merchants, soldiers, and ordinary citizens to learn to read and write.

prompt: Match each script to its origin:
explanation: Writing was independently invented several times. Cuneiform in Sumer is the earliest attested system; Egyptian hieroglyphs followed shortly after. Chinese script appears on oracle bones used for divination in the late Shang dynasty. The Phoenician alphabet, simplified from Semitic adaptations of Egyptian signs, became the ancestor of nearly all modern alphabetic scripts.

prompt: Gutenberg's most important innovation around 1450 was:
options: The first paper mill in Europe
Movable, reusable cast metal type
The first printed Bible
Reading glasses
correctAnswer: Movable, reusable cast metal type
explanation: The screw press and oil-based ink were adapted from existing technologies; Gutenberg's decisive contribution was the hand mould that cast thousands of identical, reusable letters from a metal alloy. This is what turned printing from a one-off craft (as in wood-block books) into an industrial process where a font could be reset for any text.

prompt: Why was movable type more powerful in Europe than in earlier East Asian implementations?
options: Europeans printed on paper, Asians on bamboo
Asian inks could not adhere to metal
An alphabet needs only a few hundred sorts; Chinese needs thousands
The Korean Jikji was a hoax
correctAnswer: An alphabet needs only a few hundred sorts; Chinese needs thousands
explanation: Korean printers cast metal movable type by 1377 (the Jikji), almost a century before Gutenberg. But casting and hand-setting a font of several thousand Chinese characters made the technique only marginally cheaper than block printing. With ~26 letters, an alphabetic font is dramatically more economical to cast and compose, multiplying the technique's commercial leverage.

prompt: The 1517 publication that launched the Protestant Reformation was Martin Luther's _________ Theses.
correctAnswer: Ninety-Five
explanation: Luther's Ninety-Five Theses (1517) attacked the sale of indulgences. They were academic in tone but, distributed in cheap printed pamphlets — often vernacular German — they sold an estimated 300,000 copies in three years. The Reformation became the first mass media event, demonstrating that a new printing infrastructure could outflank the Church's traditional control of religious communication.

prompt: Benedict Anderson's term 'print capitalism' refers to the way printed books and newspapers:
options: Helped imagine modern nations by standardizing vernacular languages
Made banking obsolete
Required cooperation between rival monarchs
Destroyed local dialects deliberately
correctAnswer: Helped imagine modern nations by standardizing vernacular languages
explanation: Anderson argued in 'Imagined Communities' (1983) that early printers, seeking the largest profitable market, settled on standardized written forms of vernaculars (English, French, German). Readers across a territory now consumed the same news in the same language at roughly the same time, gradually imagining themselves as members of a shared 'nation' — a community most of whose members will never meet.

prompt: Match each early-print landmark to its date:
explanation: These three dates trace the arc of the early print era: invention, disruption, and reaction. Gutenberg's Bible demonstrates the new technology; Luther's Theses prove its political potency; the Index is Rome's institutional response — a list of banned books, paired with the licensing of printers. Cheap print, mass political mobilization, and state attempts to control the channel: a pattern repeated for every new medium since.

prompt: What was Benjamin Day's central business innovation when he launched the New York Sun in 1833?
options: Distributing the paper free of charge
Funding a one-cent paper with advertising sold against a mass audience
Reporting only on financial markets
Printing in colour for the first time
correctAnswer: Funding a one-cent paper with advertising sold against a mass audience
explanation: Day priced the Sun at a single penny — affordable to ordinary New Yorkers — and funded it with advertising rather than subscriptions. To attract the mass audience advertisers wanted, the paper covered crime, scandal, and human-interest stories. The model recurred everywhere print and broadcasting went: a low cover price (or none at all), a mass audience, advertising as the real revenue source.

prompt: The terse, front-loaded news style imposed partly by per-word telegraph charges is called the inverted __________.
correctAnswer: pyramid
explanation: When news travelled by wire and every word cost money, reporters learned to put the most important facts in the first sentence and trail less essential detail behind. The 'inverted pyramid' is still the default structure of a news story: the lede answers who, what, when, where, why; later paragraphs add depth. The form is partly an aesthetic choice and partly an artefact of 19th-century telegraph economics.

prompt: One reason 'objectivity' became a journalistic ideal is that:
options: 19th-century philosophers proved it was attainable
Wire agencies sold the same copy to politically diverse papers
Governments mandated it by statute
Readers refused to buy opinionated papers
correctAnswer: Wire agencies sold the same copy to politically diverse papers
explanation: Reuters, AP, and Havas/AFP needed copy that could run in a Tory paper in London, a Republican paper in Chicago, and a left-leaning paper in Paris without offending any of them. The commercial answer was an impersonal, just-the-facts house style. Objectivity has many roots — Progressive-era reform, professionalization, and 20th-century journalism schools all contributed — but the wire bill was an early and durable one.

prompt: 'Yellow journalism' is most associated with which two publishers in 1890s New York?
options: Lincoln Steffens and Ida Tarbell
Joseph Pulitzer and William Randolph Hearst
Adolph Ochs and Charles Dana
Horace Greeley and Henry Raymond
correctAnswer: Joseph Pulitzer and William Randolph Hearst
explanation: Pulitzer's World and Hearst's Journal fought a circulation war using banner headlines, sensational crime coverage, and crusading exposés. Their treatment of the explosion of the USS Maine in 1898 is widely cited as having helped push the US into the Spanish-American War. The label 'yellow' came from the Yellow Kid comic that both papers ran. (Steffens, Tarbell, and Sinclair are muckrakers — a parallel but distinct strand.)

prompt: Match each muckraker to their target:
explanation: Tarbell's serialized History of the Standard Oil Company (1902–1904) helped justify the 1911 antitrust break-up of Rockefeller's empire. Steffens's Shame of the Cities exposed corruption in city governments. Sinclair's novel The Jungle (1906) horrified readers about Chicago meatpacking and led directly to the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act later that year. Long-form investigation became a recognised — and politically consequential — form of journalism.

prompt: What is the key difference between Marconi's early wireless and 1920s broadcasting?
options: Wireless used Morse code; broadcasting used voice
One-to-one transmission vs one-to-many
Wireless was illegal; broadcasting was licensed
Wireless used satellites; broadcasting used cables
correctAnswer: One-to-one transmission vs one-to-many
explanation: Marconi's wireless was conceived as a substitute for the telegraph — point-to-point messages, often Morse, between specific senders and receivers. The 1920s innovation was to broadcast a single transmission to anyone with a receiver in range. That shift, not voice modulation alone, made radio a mass medium and posed the regulatory question that defined 20th-century broadcasting policy: who gets to transmit, and on what terms?

prompt: John Reith's mission for the BBC was to inform, educate, and __________.
correctAnswer: entertain
explanation: John Reith, the BBC's first Director-General, defined its public-service triad as 'inform, educate, and entertain'. The phrase still appears in the BBC Charter and is used as shorthand worldwide for public-service broadcasting. The implicit contrast is with purely commercial broadcasting, which has no obligation to inform or educate beyond what advertisers will pay for.

prompt: What was the 'studio system' that defined Hollywood from the 1920s to the late 1940s?
options: Independent directors competing in an open market
Five vertically integrated firms that produced, distributed, and exhibited their own films
A government bureau that approved scripts before production
A union covering all film workers
correctAnswer: Five vertically integrated firms that produced, distributed, and exhibited their own films
explanation: MGM, Paramount, Warner Bros., RKO, and 20th Century Fox owned production lots, distribution networks, and chains of theaters. They contracted stars, writers, and directors on multi-year deals and assembled films almost industrially. The 1948 Paramount antitrust decree forced them to divest their theaters; television then ate the audience; and the studio system gradually unwound during the 1950s and 1960s.

prompt: Why did Goebbels's Propaganda Ministry subsidize cheap 'Volksempfänger' radio receivers?
options: To encourage German engineering exports
To replace newspapers with state-only radio in nearly every household
To raise revenue from radio licences
To compete with the BBC for British listeners
correctAnswer: To replace newspapers with state-only radio in nearly every household
explanation: The Volksempfänger ('people's receiver') was deliberately priced to put a radio in almost every German home and was technically restricted to receive mainly domestic stations. The aim was to make state broadcasting the dominant news source and to bypass the press, which the regime distrusted as harder to fully control. It is an early case study in pairing a mass medium with active state distribution policy.

prompt: Match each broadcasting figure or work to a description:

pairs.right: Live CBS reports from London during the Blitz
Nazi propaganda films Triumph of the Will and Olympia
US Army's Why We Fight series

explanation: All three illustrate how radio and cinema were used to shape wartime opinion. Murrow's reports — bombs audible behind his voice — drew American sympathy toward Britain before Pearl Harbor. Riefenstahl translated Nazi spectacle into film. Capra, a Hollywood director commissioned by the US Army, made films explaining the war to American soldiers. The medium did not pick a side; institutions did.

prompt: Roughly what share of US households owned a television by 1960?
options: Around 25%
Around 50%
Around 87%
Effectively 100%
correctAnswer: Around 87%
explanation: Television's diffusion was extraordinarily fast: from about 9% of US households in 1950 to roughly 87% in 1960. No medium since print had reached such a high share of households so quickly. The speed mattered: it created, almost overnight, the largest unified mass audience in history, which is the substrate for everything else about mid-20th-century broadcast culture.

prompt: What is the main funding model of public-service broadcasters such as the BBC, NHK, and ARD?
options: Direct state appropriation tied to government priorities
A household licence fee or its equivalent, with editorial independence
Voluntary donations only
Pay-per-view subscriptions
correctAnswer: A household licence fee or its equivalent, with editorial independence
explanation: The classic public-service model funds the broadcaster through a household licence fee (or the equivalent dedicated tax), insulates editorial decisions from the government of the day via a charter or board, and obliges the broadcaster to serve a wide range of citizens rather than only the demographics commercial advertisers want. The model is not perfectly clean — funding fights and political pressure recur — but it is structurally distinct from both purely commercial and purely state broadcasting.

prompt: The 24-hour news channel launched by Ted Turner in 1980 and credited with creating live cable news is __________.
correctAnswer: CNN
explanation: CNN — the Cable News Network — went on the air in June 1980 with the audacious bet that there was a 24-hour audience for news. Coverage of the 1991 Gulf War from Baghdad confirmed the format and pushed competitors to imitate. Cable's broader effect was to dismantle the three-network era: news, sports, music, and drama each got their own channel, fragmenting the mass audience that had defined 1950s and 1960s television.

prompt: Why is the 1960 Kennedy–Nixon debate often used to illustrate television's political effects?
options: It was the first debate in American history
It was rated a Kennedy win on TV and a Nixon win on radio
It was the first debate broadcast in colour
It produced the highest-rated programme of the decade
correctAnswer: It was rated a Kennedy win on TV and a Nixon win on radio
explanation: Polling after the first 1960 debate suggested radio listeners thought Nixon had performed at least as well as Kennedy, while television viewers — seeing a tanned, composed Kennedy next to a sweating, recently ill Nixon — gave Kennedy the edge. The episode is the textbook example of the medium reshaping political perception: appearance and demeanour now mattered alongside argument, and political campaigning rebuilt itself around that fact.

prompt: Match each broadcasting milestone to a description:

pairs.right: Walter Cronkite calls Vietnam a stalemate
24-hour music video, defined a visual generation

explanation: Apollo 11 shows TV's ability to gather a global mass audience. Tet shows live coverage corroding political consent for war. MTV shows cable's narrowcasting era — channels aimed at slices of the audience rather than the whole household. Together they map TV's three modes: shared spectacle, accountability, and lifestyle programming.

prompt: What is packet switching?
options: Encrypting data before transmission
Breaking a message into pieces and routing each separately across a network
Connecting two computers with a dedicated wire for each call
Switching between TV channels electronically
correctAnswer: Breaking a message into pieces and routing each separately across a network
explanation: Independently developed by Paul Baran (Rand) and Donald Davies (UK NPL) in the 1960s, packet switching breaks a message into small packets that find their own way across a redundant network and reassemble at the destination. There is no dedicated end-to-end circuit. The result is a network that scales gracefully and tolerates the loss of any individual link — properties on which the public internet still depends.

prompt: The World Wide Web was created by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989–1991 while he was working at the European physics laboratory __________.
correctAnswer: CERN
explanation: Berners-Lee designed HTML, HTTP, and the first browser at CERN to help physicists share documents across heterogeneous machines. CERN released the underlying technology into the public domain in 1993 — a decision that arguably did more to shape the modern web than any technical choice in it. The 1993 graphical Mosaic browser then made the web usable for non-specialists.

prompt: What primarily distinguishes 'Web 2.0' platforms from earlier 'Web 1.0' sites?
options: They use HTTPS instead of HTTP
They are built on user-generated content, social graphs, and ad-funded targeting
They run only on mobile devices
They require paid subscriptions
correctAnswer: They are built on user-generated content, social graphs, and ad-funded targeting
explanation: Web 1.0 was largely a publisher-to-reader model: companies and news organizations posted pages, users read them. Web 2.0 (Wikipedia, Facebook, YouTube, Twitter, Reddit) shifted the centre of gravity to user-generated content and social interaction, and funded itself by selling targeted attention to advertisers. The smartphone then put a participatory feed in every pocket. The shift was as much economic as technical.

prompt: What is the main difference between a chronological feed and an algorithmic feed?
options: Algorithmic feeds use HTTPS
Chronological feeds show posts in the order they were made; algorithmic feeds rank to maximize engagement
Algorithmic feeds are illegal under the GDPR
Chronological feeds support video; algorithmic feeds do not
correctAnswer: Chronological feeds show posts in the order they were made; algorithmic feeds rank to maximize engagement
explanation: An algorithmic feed orders posts by a machine-learned prediction of what is most likely to keep the user on the platform — clicks, dwell time, shares, replies. The shift made platforms more engaging and more politically consequential, since outrage and novelty often score well on those metrics. TikTok's For You Page is the most aggressive implementation; Facebook, Twitter/X, YouTube, and Instagram all moved in the same direction.

prompt: Match each digital-era milestone to its rough date:
explanation: ARPANET (1969) creates the technical substrate; the Web (1989–1991) makes that substrate accessible to ordinary readers and publishers; the iPhone (2007) puts the connected feed in every pocket and forces the redesign of every digital service around mobile. These three dates trace the move of the internet from research project to mass medium to ambient infrastructure.
